discussion_comments.comment_body:
We're not wrapping `ValueError`:

https://github.com/python/cpython/blob/5564790598b8bcc58c00df31a62ca56745961911/Lib/profiling/sampling/sample.py#L180

The consequence is that it kills the whole session.

```suggestion
                PyErr_Format(PyExc_RuntimeError,
```

What do you think?

Following on from the retry_config comment in the docs: in the "server has ECH keys but the cert isn't valid for public_name" case, calling this after the failed handshake raises rather than returning b"":

`ssl.SSLError: [SSL] OSSL_STORE lib (_ssl.c:2213)`

That comes from SSL_ech_get1_retry_config() refusing to release a config it received but couldn't authenticate, which is the right outcome per [RFC 9849 6.1.6](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9849/#name-handshaking-with-clienthello). But the docs for SSLSocket.get_ech_retry_config() say it returns b"" if no retry configuration is available, and the error text gives the caller nothing to go on.

fill_and_set_sslerror() already maps this same failure to an empty value for the exception attribute. Could this method do the same, so the two agree? If you'd rather keep raising, the docs should say so.

Minor, same function: config_len is uninitialized here but initialized to 0 at the other call site. OpenSSL sets it on every success path today, so this is only for consistency.
Fixed.
Escaping calls shouldn't be inside control flow statements. See https://github.com/python/cpython/pull/122693#issue-2448832631.

Addressed in the current head: `_PyEval_MonitorRaise()` is called outside the control-flow branch and its result is assigned to `err` before branching, following the escaping-call convention. The generated executor file was regenerated and verified consistent. I also added tier-2 coverage that locates `_ITER_NEXT_INLINE` and checks callback-error propagation. The tier-2 interpreter CI job and its `test_monitoring` module passed; the job summary does not expose this individual method's pass/skip result, so I am not claiming more than the logs establish. Could you please re-review when convenient?

Possible integer overflow here. Use `PyLong_AsInt()`.

And do we need an additional range check before passing it to `find_tzrule_ttinfo()` or it works with the full range of `int`?
Or use `int` and `PyLong_AsLong()` for `fold_int`.
Why do we want to continue if we're in an error state?

The `== -1 && PyErr_Occurred()`  is just the idiom the [docs recommend](https://docs.python.org/3/c-api/long.html#c.PyLong_AsLong), since `-1` is the only return value that can signal failure, any other value lets you skip the `PyErr_Occurred()` call. Not something I'd block on, feel free to leave it.

Ah, I guess that is fair. I was thinking that you might be in an error state for some other reason and bail out, but we would detect that when the function completes anyway, and it's probably better to do the cheap test in the common case.
Since we are re-calling the C API here, we need to check that `PyNumber_Subtract(a, _PyLong_GetOne())` succeeded (if I read the code correctly)
Why not use Py_XDECREF in the Done section, like all the existing replacements?
The code is now simpler. But I'm calling Py_XDECREF not just in Done, but also before calling the next make_dash_replacement to clean up its result each time.
Let's use `PyIter_NextItem`, `PyIter_Next` has a weird return value.
instead of that line, please add some assert any a small comment explaininh why we do not need to decref (e.g., say that extend steals a ref upon failure)
done

`pycore_init_builtins` still leaks `bimod` on the `_PyBuiltin_InitPythonFunctions` early return (inside `config->_install_importlib`). Also the two fixed sites should be `Py_DECREF` not `Py_XDECREF`, `bimod` is non-NULL there.

`new_interpreter`: `_PyObject_InitState` and `_PyStats_InterpInit` failure checks still `return status` instead of `goto error`, skipping `_PyThreadState_Attach`.
